{
  "need": "Competence",
  "secondary": { "name": "Identity" },
  "read": "This student put in real effort and still came up short, which is the worst-case scenario for a developing learner — it feels like proof that trying doesn't matter. The identity layer is that they're starting to write a story about themselves: 'I'm just not a math person' or 'science isn't for me.' If that story hardens, effort itself becomes the enemy because trying and failing is more painful than not trying at all.",
  "pull": { "collapse": "Protector", "instinct": "Soften the grade, say 'it's okay, you tried your best,' or pivot to praising effort alone — which accidentally confirms that the result was fine and the ceiling is real, leaving the student with no path forward." },
  "mentorMove": "Hold the standard — this content is learnable and you expect them to get there — while zeroing in on what specifically broke down in the gap between studying and performing, treating that gap as information, not a verdict.",
  "holdFirm": [
    "The material is still the goal; a poor score doesn't revise what they're expected to understand.",
    "Effort is necessary but not sufficient — how they studied is on the table now too, and that's fixable."
  ],
  "stayFlexible": [
    "Let them choose when and how they revisit the material — reteach session, office hours, a study partner, a different format.",
    "Be open to the possibility the studying method was the real problem, not the volume of effort."
  ],
  "forceLevel": { "level": 1, "label": "Empathy" },
  "script": [
    { "phase": "Connection", "words": "Hey, I noticed you looked pretty defeated after you got that back. That stings, especially when you actually put work in. I'm not brushing past that." },
    { "phase": "Curiosity", "words": "Can I ask — when you were studying, what did that actually look like? Like, walk me through what you did, because I want to understand where things went sideways, not just assume." },
    { "phase": "Collaboration", "words": "Here's what I'm seeing a lot of students run into: studying can feel productive — reading notes, highlighting — and still not be the kind of practice that translates on a test. That's not a you problem, that's a strategy problem, and strategy is something we can actually change. Let's figure out together what a different approach would look like before the next one." },
    { "phase": "Commitment", "words": "I'm not backing off what I expect you to know here, because I've watched you work and I genuinely believe you can get there — this score is not your ceiling. Pick one thing from our conversation to try differently and check in with me next week. That's the deal." }
  ],
  "longGame": "If the student starts to experience effort leading somewhere — even small, visible progress — the fixed-ability story loses its grip. Keep redirecting from 'am I smart enough' to 'what does my brain need next,' and name growth out loud every time you see it so the new story has evidence behind it."
}
situation: A student who clearly studied did poorly and is convinced they are just bad at this subject.
